derivation.title: Rigorous derivation
derivation.lead: We will need only two things, both already familiar: the definition of force as momentum transferred per second, and the mean free path. We will not postulate any separate "law of friction" — it will emerge by itself, and that is the main content of the derivation.

steps.text: Take a gas between two plates: the bottom one is stationary, the top one moves along itself. The steady flow consists of layers, each with its own average velocity u(y). Let us immediately separate two motions that occur simultaneously in the gas. Thermal motion is chaotic, equal in all directions, and very fast: hundreds of meters per second. The drift is ordered, directed along the plates, and small: centimeters per second. A molecule flies almost as in a stationary gas, but each carries a tiny addition of momentum along the flow, equal to m·u(y). This addition is precisely what all subsequent calculations will focus on.
steps.figCaption: Drift is a fine adjustment on top of chaos: the arrows of thermal motion are orders of magnitude longer

steps.text: Inside the gas, draw an imaginary area A parallel to the plates, and count how many molecules cross it per second. The count is exactly the same as in the first section of the topic: we take the simplest model of chaos, in which molecules are divided equally among the six directions of the axes, and we get one-sixth upward and one-sixth downward. A caveat that was not needed in the first section but is needed here: an honest averaging over directions gives not one-sixth but one-fourth. We take one-sixth for transparency; the analysis is in the first inset and in the appendix.
steps.latex: \Phi = \tfrac{1}{6}\, n\, \bar v \quad \text{molecules per square meter per second, in each direction}
steps.figCaption: Four directions go along the area and carry nothing through it; only two work

steps.text: Now the key question: what momentum does each molecule bring? Not the one it had initially, but the one it acquired in its last collision. A molecule crossing the area from top to bottom, on average, last collided at λ above — there it acquired the drift addition of its layer. Thus, downward it carries m·u(y+λ). The counterflow carries upward m·u(y−λ). A molecule remembers not the place where we caught it, but where it last agreed on velocity with someone.
steps.figCaption: Through the same area flow two counter-streams of molecules, but their cargoes are different

steps.text: Now assemble. The number of molecules in both directions is the same — matter does not flow anywhere, the gas does not deplete from above or below. But momentum flows, because what is brought from above and below differs. Expand the difference in small λ: even terms cancel exactly upon subtraction, and the doubled derivative remains. The resulting momentum flux per unit area is precisely the shear stress. Comparing it with Newton's law, we read off the coefficient.
steps.latex: \tau = \tfrac{1}{6} n \bar v\, m\left[u(y+\lambda)-u(y-\lambda)\right] = \tfrac{1}{3}\, n m\, \bar v \lambda\, \frac{du}{dy} \;\Longrightarrow\; \eta = \tfrac{1}{3}\rho\,\bar v\,\lambda
steps.figCaption: Friction between layers is not postulated but derived: it is simply the momentum flux across the flow

steps.text: The formula is already ready, but the most interesting part begins when we substitute the mean free path into it. It is known from the first section: λ = 1/(√2·nσ). Density is also expressed in terms of concentration: ρ = nm. Substituting both — and the concentration disappears. This is not an algebraic coincidence but a physical statement: dilute the gas by half, and the carriers of momentum become half as many, but each will carry its cargo twice as deep into the neighboring layer. The decrease in number is exactly compensated by the increase in range.
steps.figCaption: On the left, many short runs; on the right, few long ones; the product is the same

steps.text: So what then controls the viscosity of a gas? Only temperature and the type of molecules. Substitute the average velocity from the Maxwell distribution and we get an explicit dependence. Viscosity grows as the square root of absolute temperature — that is, when heated, a gas becomes THICKER. For a liquid, it is the opposite, and not just slightly: there viscosity drops exponentially, because the mechanism is completely different — molecules must squeeze past neighbors through an energy barrier. Maxwell's experiment gave an even steeper growth than the root, almost linear; today's measurements give an exponent of about 0.76. The reason for the deviation is that the cross-section σ is not constant; the analysis is in the appendix.
steps.figCaption: The two curves diverge in opposite directions because different mechanisms lie behind them

steps.text: Now let us look back at the entire topic at once. Nowhere in the derivation was there anything specifically about momentum. We counted how many molecules cross the area and multiplied by what each carries. Replace the cargo — and you get the two previous sections. If the cargo is the tagged molecule itself, we get diffusion. If it is thermal energy — thermal conductivity. If it is momentum along the flow — viscosity. The factor ⅓λ⟨v⟩ is the same in all three cases, because the carrier is the same.
steps.latex: J_G = -\tfrac{1}{3}\bar v \lambda\, \frac{d(nG)}{dy}; \qquad D = \tfrac{1}{3}\bar v\lambda, \quad \kappa = \tfrac{1}{3}\rho c_V \bar v\lambda, \quad \eta = \tfrac{1}{3}\rho \bar v\lambda
steps.figCaption: The three coefficients differ only in how much cargo there is per cubic meter of gas

steps.text: The common factor has a testable consequence. Divide viscosity by density — we get kinematic viscosity ν; divide thermal conductivity by ρc_p — we get thermal diffusivity a; the diffusion coefficient D is already ready. All three are now measured in square meters per second, so their ratios are pure numbers. The Prandtl number compares the spreading of momentum with the spreading of heat; the Schmidt number — with the spreading of an impurity. Our crude theory promises Sc = 1 and Pr = c_p/c_V = γ, i.e., 1.4 for air. Measurement gives Sc about 0.8 and Pr = 0.71: for the Prandtl number, the miss is exactly a factor of two, and this is the largest error in the section. It is fixed by a single correction. Fast molecules both cross the area more often and carry more translational energy — this correlation enhances thermal conductivity, but does not apply to the rotational energy of molecules. Accounting for the difference, Eucken obtained Pr = 4γ/(9γ−5): 0.74 for diatomic gases and 0.67 for monatomic ones — and this matches experiment. The main point survives: the ratios come out on the order of unity, not on the order of a hundred, so all three phenomena are indeed caused by a single carrier.
steps.figCaption: For gases, the Prandtl number hugs 0.7 regardless of the type; for liquids, the spread is six orders of magnitude

derivation.plateCap: Three factors: how many carriers per cubic meter, how fast they scurry, how far they carry the cargo. Change the cargo — you get diffusion or thermal conductivity, and the factor ⅓λ⟨v⟩ remains the same. All the oddity of gas viscosity is hidden in the fact that when pressure changes, density and mean free path pull in opposite directions and cancel each other out.
derivation.note: Let us list the assumptions — they are also the boundaries of the formula. First: one-sixth of the flux in each direction and the distance of the last collision exactly λ — both estimates are rough. The exact theory gives a factor of 0.499 instead of ⅓, so our answer is underestimated by about a factor of one and a half. The structure is completely correct: the dependencies on ρ, ⟨v⟩, and λ are rigorous; the error sits only in the number in front of them. Second: the collision cross-section σ was assumed constant, as for billiard balls. Real molecules are soft and attract each other, so the measured temperature dependence is steeper than the root — see the appendix. Third, and most important: everywhere it was assumed that a molecule manages to collide with another molecule before reaching the wall, i.e., λ is much smaller than both the size of the vessel and the distance over which the velocity noticeably changes. As soon as this ceases to be true, viscosity ceases to be a property of the substance and begins to depend on geometry and pressure. Fourth: the gas is rarefied in the sense that collisions are pairwise; at pressures of tens of atmospheres, a density dependence appears that is completely absent from our formula. Fifth: the drift is much smaller than the thermal velocity — otherwise it is no longer a shear of layers but a different problem.

math.title: The Math Needed Here
math.lead: Three places where a formal trick does substantive work, not just dresses up a ready answer.

items.what: Averaging over directions: where the sixth part came from and why the fourth is correct
items.why: In the second step of the derivation, we divided the molecules into six equal beams along the axes. This is not a physical statement about the gas, but a way to bypass the integral, and it's worth understanding which one. An honest calculation looks like this. The direction of velocity is equally probable in all directions, i.e., uniformly distributed over the sphere—but uniformly over the AREA of the sphere, not over the tilt angle: the weight of a direction is given by the belt sin θ dθ, and there are simply more tilted directions than those close to the axis. Through a patch, a molecule transfers a contribution proportional to the projection of velocity, i.e., cos θ, and the average must be taken over the hemisphere, because the other half flies in the opposite direction. The average cosine over the hemisphere turns out to be exactly ½, and the flux comes out to ¼n⟨v⟩ instead of our sixth part. The rule worth doing this once in your life for: when averaging over directions in three dimensions, you cannot split molecules into several equal beams—the weight is set by the solid angle. The six-beam model is good because it gives the correct structure of the formula, and bad because it gives the wrong factor in front of it.

items.what: How to check what cancels and what only seems to
items.why: In the fifth step, the concentration disappears from the answer, and this should be checked not by eye but by the exponents. Let's write out the dependence of each factor on n: density ρ = nm gives the first power, mean free path λ = 1/(√2·nσ) gives minus first, and average speed does not depend on concentration at all. The sum of exponents is zero, so the product does not depend on n. The trick is general and useful: before rejoicing at a cancellation, you must make sure that none of the remaining factors hides the same variable inside itself. Here the dangerous candidate is precisely ⟨v⟩—but it is determined by temperature and molecular mass, and does not remember concentration, so it survives. The reverse also works: if ⟨v⟩ depended on density, the whole effect would vanish, and with it the entire section.

items.what: Why the ratio of two transport coefficients is an honest number
items.why: In the eighth step, we divide viscosity by thermal diffusivity and declare the result meaningful. Dividing physical quantities by each other is not always meaningful; here it is, and this is checked by units. Kinematic viscosity ν = η/ρ, thermal diffusivity a = κ/(ρc_p), and diffusion coefficient D—all three are measured in square meters per second. The coincidence of dimensions is not accidental: each answers the same question—what area does the spreading cover per second—but different things spread. Therefore, their ratios turn out to be pure numbers that can be compared between substances and between laboratories without any conversion. The check is simple and strict: if the ratio still has a dimension, you divided the wrong thing by the wrong thing.

example.title: Example with numbers
example.lead: Let's calculate the viscosity of air from scratch and honestly compare it with the measured value. Along the way, we'll check the main claim of the section where it can be checked against a reference: at an altitude of ten kilometers.
example.given: Air at 20 °C and atmospheric pressure: density ρ = 1.20 kg/m³, mean free path λ = 68 nm, molar mass M = 29 g/mol. Find the viscosity and compare with the tabulated value 1.81·10⁻⁵ Pa·s. Then estimate the viscosity at an altitude of 10 km, where the pressure is four times lower and the temperature is 223 K.

solution.text: Mean thermal speed. We take the formula from the Maxwell distribution and keep track of which speed is needed: the mean ⟨v⟩ participates in transport, not the root-mean-square speed — they differ by eight percent, and substituting the wrong one gives a systematic error.
Substitute into the viscosity formula. It is convenient to calculate piece by piece: one third of 1.20 is 0.40; multiply by 463 — about 185; and finally multiply by 68 nanometers.

Compare with the table. We got 1.26 versus the measured 1.81 — a miss of about one and a half times. This is not a calculation error: the two geometric corrections that come to mind first cancel each other out and do not change the third. The miss is caused by correlation — fast molecules travel farther and cross the area more often, so the mean product is greater than the product of the means. The rigorous Chapman–Enskog theory gives a factor of 0.499 instead of ⅓, and with it the answer matches the measurement.

Altitude 10 km — a check of the main claim. The density there is three times lower (0.41 versus 1.225 kg/m³), but the mean free path is correspondingly larger, so the product ρλ does not change at all. Only the temperature remains: 223 K instead of 293, and the mean speed drops as the square root of their ratio.

example.answer: η ≈ 1.3·10⁻⁵ Pa·s versus the tabulated 1.81·10⁻⁵: the rough formula underestimates by a factor of one and a half, but it correctly captures the dependencies on ρ, ⟨v⟩, and λ. At an altitude of 10 km, our prediction is 1.58·10⁻⁵ Pa·s, while the reference gives 1.46·10⁻⁵.
example.check: Is this reasonable? Let's check three things. First: is a miss of one and a half times a lot or a little? For a formula in which no parameter was fitted, and the input data were the molecular size and temperature, this is very little. It is also telling that the miss is constant: if you calibrate the factor against one measurement, all other predictions — by temperature, by gas type, by pressure — will land exactly. The error is in the number, not in the structure. Second: at altitude, our prediction is overestimated by eight percent. The square-root law turned out to be too shallow — real viscosity falls with cooling more steeply than it promises, because the exponent for air is about 0.76, not 0.5. The analysis is in the appendix, along with the formula that gives 1.46·10⁻⁵ exactly. Third, and more important than the first two: the air at ten kilometers is three times rarefied, but the viscosity dropped by only twenty percent — and that entirely due to the cold, not the rarefaction. This is precisely what the section claims. Incidentally, this leads to a practical conclusion for aviation: the Reynolds number at altitude falls almost exclusively because of the density in the numerator, not because of the viscosity in the denominator.

constants.title: Constants of this section
constants.lead: Four numbers for air at room temperature. The first two are the input to the formula, the third is its check, the fourth is the summary of the entire topic in one number.

items.name: Mean free path in air (20 °C, 1 atm)
items.why: The distance a molecule travels between collisions, and at the same time the depth to which it carries someone else's momentum. It is proportional to temperature and inversely proportional to pressure, so it varies over a wide range: in a vacuum chamber it is meters, at an altitude of a hundred kilometers it is centimeters, and in a catalyst pore it does not travel nanometers at all. Everything said in this section rests on the condition that 'λ is much smaller than the dimensions of the vessel'.
items.mnemo: Keep in mind a chain of three lengths: 0.36 nm — the molecule itself, 3.4 nm — the average distance between molecules, 68 nm — the mean free path. Each step is about ten and twenty times. The molecule has plenty of space, but not so much that it doesn't collide billions of times per second.

items.name: Average thermal speed of air molecules at 20 °C
items.why: The transport coefficients include the average speed, not the root-mean-square speed of 502 m/s or the most probable speed of 410 m/s. All three are derived from the same Maxwell distribution and differ by a few percent, but you must substitute the one that appears in the derivation. It depends only on temperature and molar mass: for hydrogen at the same temperature it is four times larger, for xenon it is half.
items.mnemo: The speed of sound in air is 343 m/s — only 1.35 times less. And this is not a coincidence: sound is carried by the same molecules with the same thermal motion, so it cannot outrun them in principle.

items.name: Dynamic viscosity of air at 20 °C
items.why: The number we compared our calculation with. The main thing about it is not the value itself, but the direction of change: at 0 °C the viscosity of air is 1.72·10⁻⁵, at 100 °C it is already 2.17·10⁻⁵ — an increase of a quarter. Water over the same interval becomes six times more fluid. Two substances, one temperature scale, opposite signs — and this is the best argument that the mechanisms are different.
items.mnemo: Eighteen micropascal-seconds. Water has a thousand — exactly fifty-five times more. Easy to remember and useful: in problems on blowing and on pipes, these two numbers are needed constantly.

items.name: Prandtl number for air
items.why: The summary of the entire topic in one number: momentum and heat spread through the gas almost equally fast, because they are carried by the same carrier. Remarkably, this number is almost independent of the type of gas: for hydrogen it is 0.70, for xenon 0.68, although the masses of their molecules differ by a factor of sixty-five. Liquids have no such constancy — from 0.025 for mercury to tens of thousands for glycerin.
items.mnemo: Zero point seven — and for the lightest gas and the heaviest. A number that does not remember what the gas is made of, because it remembers only the mechanism.

synthesis.title: How this relates to the rest of the course
synthesis.lead: This section closes the topic from within and connects with two neighboring ones — with molecular physics behind and with hydrodynamics ahead.

items.h: The first two sections of this topic
items.text: The trio of coefficients has closed: diffusion transfers particles, thermal conductivity transfers energy, viscosity transfers momentum, and all three have the same factor ⅓λ⟨v⟩. This gives a way to check yourself that did not exist when the phenomenon was alone. Measure two of the three coefficients, divide — and you get a number that the theory predicts in advance. If it is of order one, the mechanism is guessed; if it is of order a hundred, you have missed something.

items.h: Liquids and gases in motion
items.text: There, viscosity entered Newton's law, Poiseuille's formula, and the Reynolds number as a tabulated property of the substance. Now it is calculated, and along the way the paradox from that section is explained: kinematically, air is fifteen times more viscous than water. The reason is directly visible from the formula — for a gas, η is small, but ρ is even smaller, and the ratio η/ρ = ⅓λ⟨v⟩ for a rarefied medium turns out to be larger. Also, it is clear why for a gas the kinematic viscosity depends on pressure, but the dynamic viscosity does not: in ν, the density stands separately and no longer cancels.

items.h: Molecules and temperature
items.text: The average speed is taken from the Maxwell distribution, the mean free path from the collision cross-section; the same apparatus that gave the equation of state. But there is also a fundamental difference worth noting. An ideal gas in equilibrium has no gradients, and there is nothing to transfer. Transport phenomena are the first, weakest deviation from equilibrium, and the entire kinetic theory of transport lives in this narrow band: the deviation already exists, but it is still linear.

items.h: Vacuum and microtechnology
items.text: As soon as the mean free path grows to the size of the gap, viscosity ceases to be a property of the substance. Hence the design of the thermos, the calculation of vacuum systems, the behavior of microelectromechanical mirrors with micron gaps, and the aerodynamics of a descent vehicle at an altitude of a hundred kilometers. The criterion is the same — the Knudsen number, the ratio of λ to the characteristic size.

curiosities.title: Fun fact: try it with your own hands
curiosities.lead: You can't catch gas viscosity in the kitchen: air is too thin, and its viscosity is too small. But the second half of the statement—how a liquid behaves when heated—is easy to observe. The opposite sign is precisely the main result of this section.

items.h: Water and oil, cold and warm
items.text: You'll need two cocktail straws of the same diameter, water, and vegetable oil. The straw is essential: through a wide opening, liquid flows due to inertia, and viscosity hardly matters, but in a narrow channel Poiseuille's law applies, and the flow time is directly proportional to viscosity. Pour 20 ml of each liquid into identical cups, put half in the refrigerator and half in warm water (about 40 °C), and let them sit for an hour to equilibrate. Then let each flow out through the straw and time it. Question in advance: for which liquid will heating change the time more—water or oil?
items.answer: Oil, and by a large margin. Water at 5 °C has a viscosity of 1.52 mPa·s, at 40 °C—0.65 mPa·s, so the flow time changes roughly twofold. Oil over the same interval goes from about 150 mPa·s to 30 mPa·s—a fivefold change. From these numbers, you can extract the barrier energy using the Arrhenius formula: for water it comes out to about 17 kJ per mole, for oil about 33. The long molecules of oil are more entangled with each other, and squeezing past neighbors is harder—hence the higher temperature sensitivity. Now mentally repeat the same experiment with air. Heating from 5 to 40 °C increases its viscosity by about nine percent: air becomes THICKER. You can't feel this in any kitchen container, but in calculations of radiator airflow or in the aerodynamics of hot exhaust, that's exactly the sign you need.

items.h: Ball in honey, cold and heated
items.text: In the section on flows, we compared a ball in honey with a ball in water; here we change the liquid, not the temperature. Take two identical clear jars of liquid honey, put one in the refrigerator and the other in warm water no hotter than 40 degrees (above that, honey spoils). Let them sit for an hour, measure the temperature of both. Mark two lines 10 cm below the surface with a marker, and drop an identical metal ball into each—a bearing ball about 4 mm in diameter works. Time the fall between the marks. Question: how many times faster will the ball go in warm honey—twice, five times, or twenty times?
items.answer: About twenty to thirty times, and this is the most convincing result of all the kitchen experiments in this section. According to Stokes' law, the speed is inversely proportional to viscosity, so the time is directly proportional to it. Honey at 10 °C has a viscosity of about 40 Pa·s, at 40 °C—about 1.5. Heating by just thirty degrees, yet the difference is almost thirtyfold: that's the exponential in action; a power law cannot do that. Calculate the barrier energy using Arrhenius—you'll get about 85 kJ per mole, roughly equivalent to four hydrogen bonds. That's how much a sugar molecule needs to break to squeeze past its neighbors. Compare with a gas: to increase air viscosity thirtyfold, you'd have to heat it to several hundred thousand kelvins, and even then it would turn into plasma first. One experiment, two opposite physics.

items.h: Helium is seven times lighter than air—and more viscous
items.text: The molar mass of helium is 4 versus 29 for air. The molecule is light, flies faster than all others, and seeps through any crack first—you'd think it should have the weakest braking. However, the measured viscosity of helium at room temperature is 1.96·10⁻⁵ Pa·s versus 1.81·10⁻⁵ for air: helium is more viscous. How does this fit with the formula?
items.answer: It fits right into it. In the expression η = 2√(mkT/π)/(3σ), mass and cross-section pull in opposite directions, and for helium, the cross-section wins. The lightness gives a factor √(4/29) ≈ 0.37—helium should be 2.7 times LESS viscous. But the helium atom is also small: its effective diameter is 0.22 nm versus 0.37 nm for air molecules, so the cross-section σ = πd² is smaller by a factor of (0.22/0.37)² ≈ 0.35, and it's in the denominator. The result: 0.37 / 0.35 ≈ 1.05—helium turns out to be about five percent more viscous than air; the reference gives eight. This estimate can't be more precise: the effective diameters of molecules are themselves known to within a few percent, and they enter squared. Test yourself on argon: it's heavier than air (√(40/29) = 1.17), but the diameter is almost the same, and the viscosity comes out to 2.1·10⁻⁵ versus the tabulated 2.2·10⁻⁵. Separately, it's worth distinguishing two reputations of helium. Through a hole the size of a molecule or through a thick layer of rubber, helium indeed escapes faster than anything: there, it's not viscosity but thermal speed and atomic size that matter. But through a long channel where flow is viscous, helium under the same pressure difference goes slightly SLOWER than air. A balloon deflates not because helium is fluid, but because it seeps through the rubber.

items.h: Molecular size from viscosity—Loschmidt's path
items.text: The formula can be turned backwards. Measured viscosity gives the mean free path, the mean free path gives the collision cross-section, and the cross-section gives the molecular diameter. Try to go through the chain yourself: η = 1.81·10⁻⁵ Pa·s, ρ = 1.2 kg/m³, ⟨v⟩ = 463 m/s, concentration n = p/kT = 2.5·10²⁵ m⁻³.
items.answer: λ = 3η/(ρ⟨v⟩) ≈ 9.8·10⁻⁸ m; σ = 1/(√2·nλ) ≈ 2.9·10⁻¹⁹ m²; d = √(σ/π) ≈ 3.0·10⁻¹⁰ m, i.e., 0.3 nanometers. The reference value for nitrogen is 0.37 nm. The miss is smaller than the uncertainty in the viscosity itself—and that's no coincidence: the diameter is extracted from it under a square root, so an error in the factor ⅓ is halved in the exponent. Exactly this chain was followed by Josef Loschmidt in 1865, adding a second equation—the density of liquid air, which gives the number of molecules times the cube of the diameter. From two equations, he found both the size and the concentration: about one nanometer and roughly 1.8·10¹⁸ molecules per cubic centimeter. The diameter was overestimated threefold, the concentration underestimated fifteenfold—the first ever estimate of atomic size missed by only an order of magnitude, even though half the physicists of that time didn't believe atoms existed at all.

items.h: Unity for gases, six orders of magnitude for liquids
items.text: The Prandtl number for any gas is about 0.7 and almost independent of the species. For liquids, it ranges from 0.025 for mercury to tens of thousands for glycerin. Where does such a chasm between the two states of matter come from?
items.answer: Because in a gas, all three transfers are carried by the same carrier—a freely flying molecule—and in each coefficient, the same factor ⅓λ⟨v⟩ appears. Their ratio is bound to be a number of order unity, and it is. In a dense liquid, the carriers are different. Momentum is transferred through direct interaction between neighbors, heat too, but in a liquid metal, the main heat carrier becomes the conduction electrons; we discussed them in the second section, where we derived the Lorenz number. Electrons have nothing to do with viscosity. Hence mercury: heat travels much faster than momentum. Glycerin has the opposite skew—viscosity is huge, but thermal conductivity is ordinary. The practical conclusion for an engineer is harsh: correlation formulas for heat transfer obtained with air cannot be transferred to liquid sodium in a reactor—there, it's different physics, not a different value of a coefficient. And an honest caveat: a general theory of transport in dense liquids, comparable in rigor to the kinetic theory of gases, has not been constructed to this day. For gases, we calculate coefficients from first principles; for liquids, we measure and fit.

appendix.title: What we glossed over and how it is fixed

blocks.h: The factor ⅓: where the 1.5-fold miss came from
blocks.text: There were three simplifications, and the first two are not errors in the same direction but a pair that cancels out. First: we assumed that molecules fly strictly along the axes and got a flux of ⅙n⟨v⟩ in each direction; an honest calculation over angles gives ¼n⟨v⟩ — 1.5 times more. Second: the distance from which a molecule brings foreign momentum we took to be λ, but it arrives at an angle, and the projection of this distance onto the normal is on average ⅔λ — that many times less. One and a half times two-thirds gives one: a careful angular calculation returns exactly our third, and the miss remains unexplained. The third, subtlest simplification explains it: fast molecules both travel farther and cross the area more often, so averaging the product as the product of averages is not allowed — this correlation again works to increase. The rigorous solution of the Boltzmann equation for hard spheres, obtained by Chapman and Enskog independently during World War I, gives a closed formula. Numerically it corresponds to a factor of 0.499 instead of our third, that is, exactly the discrepancy we measured in air.

blocks.h: Sutherland's formula: why not a square root
blocks.text: Our dependence η ∝ √T came from a single assumption — that the collision cross-section σ is constant, like billiard balls. Real molecules attract each other on approach, and the trajectory of a slow molecule bends more: it grazes a neighbor even when geometrically it would have passed by. Therefore, the effective cross-section is larger than the geometric one, and the colder the gas, the larger. With heating, attraction loses importance, σ decreases, and viscosity grows faster than the square root. In 1893, Sutherland reduced this correction to a single constant S with the dimension of temperature — essentially, the depth of attraction in degrees. For air, S ≈ 111 K. The formula holds for air from cryogenic temperatures to one and a half thousand kelvins with accuracy within a few percent: at 0 °C it gives 1.72·10⁻⁵, at 20 °C — 1.81·10⁻⁵, at 100 °C — 2.17·10⁻⁵, and at an altitude of ten kilometers those same 1.46·10⁻⁵ that our square root did not give. The effective exponent comes out to about 0.76 — between the square root and unity. Maxwell in his narrow range measured exactly unity and built a model of molecules repelling as the fifth power of distance; the model turned out to be more durable than the measurement that gave birth to it.

blocks.h: Knudsen number: four regimes instead of one
blocks.text: Everything stated is valid as long as a molecule collides with other molecules more often than with walls. The measure is the ratio of the mean free path to the characteristic size. At Kn less than 0.01, the gas behaves as a continuous medium: everything we derived holds, and the no-slip condition applies at the wall. From 0.01 to 0.1, the slip regime occurs: the gas near the wall already slips, and the no-slip condition must be corrected by a correction proportional to λ. From 0.1 to 10, the transition regime is the most inconvenient: neither kinetic theory in our form nor continuum equations work, and direct simulation of collisions by the Monte Carlo method is used. Above 10, the free-molecular regime sets in: molecules fly from wall to wall, the concept of viscosity as a property of matter loses meaning, and momentum transfer becomes directly proportional to pressure. For thermal conductivity, this same transition was discussed in the second section using the thermos example; for viscosity, it is important in other places. Microelectromechanical mirrors with gaps of a micron: at atmospheric pressure, Kn there is about 0.07 — already the slip regime, and damping is calculated with a correction. Vacuum systems where viscous flow changes to molecular and the formulas for pump calculations change entirely. Descent of a spacecraft from orbit: at an altitude of one hundred kilometers, λ is measured in centimeters, at one hundred fifty — in meters, and familiar aerodynamics does not work there at all. Finally, thin lubricant films and catalyst pores, where the gap is comparable to the mean free path even at ordinary pressure.

The general conclusion from the three corrections is the same, and it is worth keeping in mind separately from the formulas. The kinetic theory of gases is remarkable not for its accuracy but for predicting the STRUCTURE of dependencies without fitting a single parameter: how viscosity depends on pressure (not at all), on temperature (increases), on the mass of the molecule and its size. It gives numerical factors with an accuracy of up to 1.5 times, and they are refined either by rigorous theory or by a single measurement. This is the typical order of things in physics: first the mechanism and power laws, then the coefficients.

memo.essence: Gas viscosity is the transfer of momentum across the flow by molecules flying between collisions, not a separate friction force. The coefficient is assembled from three factors: η = ⅓ρ⟨v⟩λ. This leads to two non-obvious consequences: gas viscosity does not depend on pressure, because density cancels with the mean free path, and it increases with heating roughly as √T — whereas for liquids it falls exponentially. The same λ and ⟨v⟩ give the diffusion coefficient and thermal conductivity: three transport phenomena — one picture with different cargo.

keyIdeas.title: Three factors instead of a table
keyIdeas.text: η = ⅓ρ⟨v⟩λ: how many carriers per cubic meter, how fast they dart, how far they carry someone else's momentum

keyIdeas.title: Pressure is irrelevant
keyIdeas.text: Pump out half — half as many carriers, but each goes twice as far. The product ρλ does not depend on concentration

keyIdeas.title: Gas thickens, liquid thins
keyIdeas.text: √T versus exp(E/kT). These are different mechanisms, not different coefficients in one formula

keyIdeas.title: Everything hinges on smallness of λ
keyIdeas.text: As soon as the mean free path grows to the gap size, viscosity ceases to be a property of the substance and remembers pressure

where: Vacuum technology: viscous flow gives way to molecular flow when λ grows to the tube diameter
High-altitude aerodynamics: air at 10 km is three times rarer, but viscosity is almost the same — Re drops due to density
Heat transfer calculations: Pr ≈ 0.7 for any gas, so formulas obtained on air transfer to other gases
Orbital reentry and micromechanics: the Knudsen number decides whether the concept of viscosity is applicable at all
memo.watchOut: Three errors are more common than others. The first is transferring kitchen intuition to gas: “hotter means thinner” is true for liquids and false for gases, the mechanisms are different and the sign is opposite. The second is considering the factor ⅓ exact: it underestimates the answer by about one and a half times, and if the task requires a number, not a structure, you need to take tabulated η or Sutherland's formula. The third, most dangerous, is applying η where the mean free path is comparable to the gap size: in vacuum technology, in microchannels, and at high altitudes, viscosity ceases to be a property of the substance and begins to depend on geometry.

quiz.q: Half of the air was pumped out of a vessel, the temperature was not changed. What happened to the viscosity of the remaining gas?
options: It did not change
It dropped by half: there are half as many carrier molecules
It doubled: molecules have more room to fly
It dropped by four: collisions are rarer and density is lower
quiz.why: In the formula η = ⅓ρ⟨v⟩λ, the density dropped by half, but the mean free path λ = 1/(√2·nσ) doubled: there are fewer carriers, but each one carries momentum twice as deep into the neighboring layer. The product ρλ does not depend on concentration at all, and the average speed is determined only by temperature. It was precisely this conclusion that Maxwell found incredible in 1860 and six years later verified by experiment with oscillating glass disks — the viscosity remained constant over the entire accessible range of pressures. One caveat: this holds as long as λ is much smaller than the vessel dimensions; in deep vacuum, a dependence on pressure appears, and that is a different regime, discussed in the appendix.
quiz.hint: Write down how each factor in η = ⅓ρ⟨v⟩λ depends on the molecular concentration n, and add up the exponents.

quiz.q: Why does the viscosity of a gas increase with heating, while the viscosity of a liquid decreases?
options: In a gas, momentum is carried by freely flying molecules, and their thermal speed increases with temperature; in a liquid, molecules are packed closely, and heating makes it easier for them to squeeze past neighbors
In a gas, density increases with heating, while in a liquid it decreases
In a gas, the mean free path increases with heating, while in a liquid it decreases
These are different quantities: for a gas, viscosity is measured by the damping of oscillations, and for a liquid by the flow rate through a tube
quiz.why: The different sign comes not from different coefficients, but from different mechanisms. In a gas, the carrier of momentum is a flying molecule, and viscosity inherits the temperature dependence of its speed: ⟨v⟩ ∝ √T, so η also increases. In a liquid, there is no free path at all; molecules are in contact, and the shear of layers requires a molecule to squeeze past its neighbors through an energy barrier; the probability of this obeys a Boltzmann factor, so viscosity decreases exponentially with heating. The option about density rising with heating is simply factually wrong: when heated in an open vessel, density decreases for both. The option about the mean free path substitutes the mechanism with a consequence — at constant density, λ does not depend on temperature at all, and for a liquid this quantity is undefined. The option that declares gas and liquid viscosity to be different quantities is factually wrong: both measurement methods give the same quantity, and this is what ensures the consistency of tables.
quiz.hint: Ask yourself what exactly carries momentum in each of the two cases — and what changes with heating for the carrier.

quiz.q: In your own words: why are the diffusion coefficient, thermal conductivity, and viscosity of a gas expressed through the same product λ·⟨v⟩?
quiz.why: Because in all three cases the same mechanism works: a molecule flies from collision to collision and carries with it what it possessed at the place of the last collision. Only the cargo changes — the molecule itself as a tag gives diffusion, its thermal energy gives thermal conductivity, its momentum along the flow gives viscosity. Therefore, each coefficient contains the factor ⅓λ⟨v⟩ — essentially, 'what area the carrier covers per second' — and the coefficients differ only in how much cargo per cubic meter: unity for the number of particles, ρc for energy, ρ for momentum. From this follows a testable prediction: the ratios of the coefficients are numbers of order unity, and for gases Pr and Sc indeed lie around 0.7–1.
quiz.hint: Analyze what is common and what differs in all three phenomena. The mechanism is the same — but what exactly does the molecule carry with it across the layer boundary?

quiz.q: Estimate the mean free path of air molecules at a pressure of 10⁻³ atmospheres and room temperature. At atmospheric pressure it is 68 nm. Answer in micrometers.
quiz.why: The mean free path λ = 1/(√2·nσ) is inversely proportional to concentration, and concentration at constant temperature is proportional to pressure. Thus λ ∝ 1/p: a thousandfold decrease in pressure increases the path exactly a thousandfold, from 68 nm to 68 μm. A common-sense estimate: 68 micrometers is already the thickness of a human hair, so in a channel a tenth of a millimeter wide, gas at such pressure would cease to be a continuous medium, and the concept of viscosity could not be applied. Hence the vacuum engineer's practical rule: as long as the path is smaller than the pipe diameter, gas is pumped in viscous flow, but once it exceeds it, it becomes molecular flow, and calculations must use different formulas.
quiz.hint: Molecular concentration at constant temperature is proportional to pressure, and mean free path is inversely proportional to concentration. By what factor did the pressure drop?

formula.name: Viscosidad del gas según la teoría cinética
formula.alsoKnown: La independencia de la viscosidad del gas respecto a la presión se denomina ley de Maxwell. Junto con D = ⅓λ⟨v⟩ y κ = ⅓ρc⟨v⟩λ, esta fórmula forma el trío de coeficientes de transporte.

authors.what: introdujo el concepto de camino libre medio: la distancia que recorre una molécula entre colisiones; sin él, en la teoría cinética no se podía decir nada cuantitativo.
dedujo que la viscosidad de un gas no depende de su densidad, y él mismo consideró el resultado poco plausible.

authors.who: James Clerk Maxwell y Katherine Maxwell
authors.what: realizaron un experimento con discos de vidrio oscilantes en un recipiente evacuado y confirmaron la independencia de la presión; además, midieron el aumento de la viscosidad con la temperatura.
invirtió la fórmula: a partir de la viscosidad medida obtuvo el camino libre medio, y de ahí la primera estimación histórica del tamaño de las moléculas.
propuso una corrección que explica por qué la viscosidad crece más rápido que la raíz cuadrada de la temperatura: la sección eficaz de colisión depende de la energía.
construyeron de forma independiente una teoría rigurosa del transporte en gases y obtuvieron factores numéricos exactos en lugar de estimaciones.

formula.story: En 1859, Maxwell, entonces profesor en Aberdeen, leyó el trabajo de Clausius sobre el camino libre medio y se propuso llevar la teoría cinética a números. En su obra 'Explicaciones sobre la teoría dinámica de los gases' obtuvo un resultado que él mismo calificó de poco plausible: la viscosidad de un gas no debería depender de su densidad. Maxwell admitió honestamente que el único experimento que conocía parecía no confirmarlo, y dejó la cuestión abierta durante seis años. Decidió comprobarlo él mismo, ya en Londres. El montaje: tres discos de vidrio horizontales suspendidos por un hilo de torsión, oscilando entre discos fijos dentro de una campana evacuada. La viscosidad del aire se medía por la amortiguación de las oscilaciones. La dificultad no era el vacío, sino la temperatura: para separar el efecto de la presión y el calentamiento, había que mantener la habitación a una temperatura fija durante horas, desde fresca hasta una en la que es difícil estar. Katherine Maxwell se encargaba de la estufa y las calderas; en las cartas de ese verano, Maxwell describía el laboratorio doméstico como un lugar donde estaba condenado al calor. El resultado de 1866: la viscosidad no cambiaba al variar la presión en varias decenas de veces. Pero el segundo resultado resultó más importante que el primero. La viscosidad aumentaba con la temperatura más rápido de lo que predecía su propia teoría: no como la raíz de T, sino aproximadamente como T. El modelo de moléculas como bolas de billar no podía explicar eso. Maxwell lo reemplazó por un modelo de partículas que se repelen con una fuerza que disminuye como la quinta potencia de la distancia; para esa ley, las ecuaciones de transporte se resuelven exactamente, y las 'moléculas de Maxwell' siguen siendo un ejemplo didáctico. La ironía es que mediciones posteriores en un amplio rango dieron un exponente de aproximadamente 0,76, entre la raíz y la unidad, es decir, la medición que dio origen al modelo no era del todo precisa. Sin embargo, el modelo sobrevivió a su creador.

symbols.note: la misma magnitud que en la ley de Newton τ = η·dv/dy del tema de flujos; aquí no la tomamos de una tabla, sino que la calculamos.
también es nm: concentración de moléculas multiplicada por la masa de una; en la fórmula representa 'cuántos portadores hay en un metro cúbico'.

cuán lejos transporta una molécula el impulso ajeno antes de cederlo en una colisión; para el aire a presión atmosférica es 68 nm.
para el aire, 4,8·10⁻²⁶ kg: la masa molar de 29 g/mol dividida por el número de Avogadro.
